questions.question: 1. How do you describe an array?

answers.a: A data structure in which accessing any element always takes linear time
answers.b: A data structure containing elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations
answers.c: A container that stores only unique elements of the same type
answers.d: A data structure whose elements are always stored at unrelated memory locations

explanations.a: Incorrect. Direct access to an array element using its index does not require traversing all preceding elements.
explanations.b: Correct. An array stores elements of the same data type in contiguous memory locations, allowing direct access using an index.
explanations.c: Incorrect. An array can contain duplicate values; uniqueness is not a property of arrays.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The elements of a conventional array are stored in contiguous memory locations.

questions.question: 2. What is the time complexity of traversing through all the elements in an array of size $N$?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A single traversal visits each element once rather than performing a nested set of $N$ operations.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The amount of work grows with the number of elements that must be visited.
explanations.c: Correct. Traversing an array of size $N$ requires visiting all $N$ elements once, giving a time complexity of $O(N)$.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Logarithmic time would require reducing the search space by a constant factor at each step, which a complete traversal does not do.

questions.question:
3. Let us consider the following code:
int a = 0, b[N];
for (i = 0; i < M; i++) {
    a += i;
}
for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    scanf("%d", &b[i]);
    a += b[i];
}
What are the space and time complexities of the above code?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The first loop does not allocate an additional data structure of size $M$; it only performs repeated operations.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The loops execute sequentially rather than being nested, so their running times do not multiply.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The array $b$ requires space proportional to $N$, and the second loop contributes to the running time.
explanations.d: Correct. The array $b$ requires $O(N)$ space, while the two sequential loops take $O(M)$ and $O(N)$ time, giving $O(M+N)$ overall time.

questions.question:
4. Let us consider the following four arrays:
A = [9, 5, 11, 25, 7, 35]
B = [1, 2, 9, 15, 27]
C = [29, 27, 27, 18, 4, 2]
D = [1, 8, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
Which of the arrays are sorted in either ascending or descending order?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Array A is not sorted because its elements do not consistently increase or decrease.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Array D is not sorted because the value 8 is followed by 2.
explanations.c: Correct. B is sorted in ascending order and C is sorted in descending order, allowing equal adjacent values in the non-increasing sequence.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Neither A nor D maintains a consistent ascending or descending order.

questions.question: 5. If, for large inputs, algorithm X is a better choice than algorithm Y, then which statement best describes their asymptotic efficiency?

answers.a: Y is asymptotically more efficient than X
answers.b: X is asymptotically more efficient than Y
answers.c: X and Y must have exactly the same asymptotic complexity
answers.d: The asymptotic efficiency of X and Y cannot be compared

explanations.a: Incorrect. This statement contradicts the condition that X is the better choice for large inputs.
explanations.b: Correct. If X is preferred for sufficiently large inputs because of its growth rate, X is asymptotically more efficient than Y.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Two algorithms with the same asymptotic complexity can still differ in constants, but having the same complexity is not required for X to be the better choice.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The statement about large inputs can be used to compare the asymptotic growth of the algorithms.

questions.question: 6. In an unsorted array, which search technique can be used without first rearranging the elements?

answers.d: No search technique can be used

explanations.a: Correct. Linear search can inspect elements one by one and does not require the array to be sorted.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The standard binary search procedure relies on the elements being ordered.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Interpolation search also relies on an ordered array and an appropriate distribution of values.
explanations.d: Incorrect. An unsorted array can still be searched using methods that do not require ordering.

questions.question: 7. What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for a particular value in an unsorted array of size $N$ using linear search?

explanations.a: Incorrect. In the worst case, the search may need to inspect many elements.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Linear search does not reduce the remaining search space logarithmically.
explanations.c: Correct. In the worst case, every element may need to be checked, giving $O(N)$ time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single linear traversal does not require a quadratic number of comparisons.

questions.question: 8. Which property of an array allows direct access to an element using its index?

answers.b: The elements are stored in contiguous memory locations
answers.d: The array is always dynamically resized

explanations.a: Incorrect. An array can provide direct indexed access even when its elements are completely unsorted.
explanations.b: Correct. Contiguous storage allows the address of an element to be calculated directly from its index and the element size.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Duplicate values do not prevent indexed access.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Dynamic resizing is not the reason array indexing provides direct access.

questions.question: 9. An unsorted array contains $N$ elements. Which statement about finding whether a particular value exists in the array is correct when no additional information about the data is available?

answers.a: The value can always be found in $O(1)$ time
answers.b: The value can always be found in $O(\log N)$ time
answers.c: A search may need to inspect all $N$ elements
answers.d: The array must be sorted before any search can be performed

explanations.a: Incorrect. Without an additional indexing structure or other information, the position of the value cannot generally be determined immediately.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Logarithmic search requires useful ordering or another structure that reduces the search space.
explanations.c: Correct. In an unsorted array, the desired value may be the last element or may be absent, so all $N$ elements may need to be inspected.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Searching is possible without sorting, although the search may require linear time.
